properties.vocals: Breathy, emotive tenor with an often fragile falsetto; uses close-mic intimacy, ornamented phrasing and electronic processing. Capable of plaintive crooning, urgent belting and manipulated/processed vocal textures for experimental effects.
properties.biography: Born in Wellingborough in 1968, Thom Yorke grew up in Oxfordshire and attended Abingdon School, where he met future Radiohead bandmates. The group — originally called On a Friday — rose from the UK indie scene to worldwide fame after the breakthrough single "Creep" (1992) and later critical milestones including OK Computer (1997) and Kid A (2000). Alongside Radiohead Yorke has released solo albums (notably The Eraser, Tomorrow's Modern Boxes and ANIMA), led the side-project Atoms For Peace, composed film music and collaborated with electronic artists. His career has been marked by musical reinvention, an embrace of electronic production, and outspoken engagement with political and environmental issues.
properties.known_for: Distinctive plaintive falsetto and emotive vocals, restless musical experimentation blending electronic and rock elements, complex arrangements and politically conscious stances.
properties.description: Thom Yorke is an English musician, singer and songwriter best known as the principal vocalist, principal songwriter and frontman of Radiohead. Beyond the band he has a solo career and fronted the electronic/experimental project Atoms for Peace; his work fuses melancholic melodies, adventurous electronic production and unconventional song structures. Yorke is noted for his plaintive, breathy falsetto, his interest in technology and politics, and for pushing the boundaries between rock and electronic music.
properties.cultural_impact: Yorke reshaped late-90s/2000s alternative music by integrating experimental electronic production with rock songwriting (notably on Kid A), influencing a generation of indie and electronic artists. He helped popularize alternative distribution approaches (Radiohead's In Rainbows pay-what-you-want release) and has been a visible advocate on environmental and political issues, extending his cultural influence beyond music.
properties.performance_style: Typically restrained and emotionally intense: intimate vocal delivery, minimal to dense electronic backdrops, dynamic build-ups, occasional theatrical movement; often uses live manipulation and improvisation with electronic elements.

properties.lyrical_themes_description: Yorke's lyrics frequently explore personal alienation, the dislocating effects of technology and modern life, political and environmental anxieties, and intimate emotional states. His writing often mixes oblique imagery with direct protest and bleak, dystopian perspectives.

properties.vocals: Often conversational and slightly nasal with flexible delivery; shifts between talk-sung verses, falsetto crooning and plaintive melodic lines. Vocals can be intimate and fragile (Sea Change) or exuberant and rhythmic (Odelay/Midnite Vultures), and are frequently treated or layered in production.
properties.biography: Born Bek David Campbell on July 8, 1970 in Los Angeles, Beck grew up exposed to a wide variety of music and visual art through his parents; his mother Bibbe Hansen was involved in the L.A. art scene and his grandfather, fluxus artist Al Hansen, influenced Beck's collage aesthetic. After dropping out of high school he traveled, lived in New York's anti-folk scene and returned to Los Angeles where early lo-fi releases and singles like the indie 12" of "Loser" (1993) sparked major-label interest. Signed to Geffen, Beck released Mellow Gold (1994) and achieved mainstream breakthrough, then broadened and subverted expectations with acclaimed albums Odelay (1996), Mutations (1998), Midnite Vultures (1999), Sea Change (2002) and later Morning Phase (2014) and Colors (2017). Over a multi-decade career he has combined sampling, live instrumentation and diverse production collaborators while continually reinventing his sound.
properties.known_for: Genre-blending songwriting and production, inventive sampling and collage aesthetics, ironic and poetic lyrics, and critically acclaimed albums spanning alternative rock, folk and experimental pop.
properties.description: Beck Hansen is an American singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist celebrated for eclectic, genre-blending music that mixes folk, hip-hop, electronic, rock and experimental pop. Rising from the early-90s anti-folk and underground scenes in Los Angeles and New York, he broke into the mainstream with the 1994 hit "Loser" and consolidated critical and commercial success with albums such as Odelay, Sea Change, Morning Phase and Colors. His work is marked by inventive sampling, ironic and poetic lyrics, diverse production approaches and frequent collaborations with producers and guest musicians.
properties.cultural_impact: Beck helped define 1990s alternative culture with a postmodern, sample-forward approach that blended hip-hop, folk, rock and electronic elements. His success made eclectic genre-mixing commercially viable and influenced indie and mainstream artists; albums like Odelay and Sea Change are widely cited by critics and musicians, and Morning Phase earned him Grammys, cementing his long-term cultural and critical stature.
properties.performance_style: Varies from intimate, acoustic-focused sets to high-energy, sample-and-band-driven performances; frequently changes arrangements, incorporates improvisation and visual/artistic elements, and often tours with rotating collaborators.
artists_influenced: Beck Hansen's contemporaries and numerous indie acts

He frequently explores alienation, romantic failure and the absurdities of modern/consumer culture, moving between humorous detachment and frank melancholy depending on the album's tone.

properties.vocals: Arcade Fire uses multiple vocalists—primarily Win Butler (raw, emotive baritone/tenor) and Régine Chassagne (breathy, vibrato-rich higher register)—often layering voices for sing-along, choral effects. Their vocals range from intimate spoken-sung lines to full-throated, anthemic group chants.
properties.biography: Formed in Montreal in the early 2000s around principal songwriter and frontman Win Butler and his wife Régine Chassagne, Arcade Fire grew from a close-knit group of musicians into an internationally acclaimed ensemble. Early demos and local shows led to their debut album, Funeral (2004), which combined intimate lyrics about loss and youth with sweeping, orchestral arrangements and launched them beyond the Canadian scene. Over successive albums they expanded their sonic palette—adding synths, dance rhythms and art-rock textures—while maintaining a focus on communal, emotionally charged songs and ambitious live staging.
properties.known_for: Anthemic, emotionally charged songs built from orchestral and multi-instrumental arrangements, theatrical live performances, and conceptually ambitious albums.
properties.description: Arcade Fire is a Montreal-based Canadian indie rock band celebrated for large-scale, anthemic songs, lush orchestration, and multi-instrumental arrangements. Emerging in the early 2000s, they blend rock, chamber pop and experimental textures into emotionally direct music and theatrical live performances. Their albums (notably Funeral and The Suburbs) combined intimate songwriting with dramatic crescendos and earned widespread critical and commercial success.
properties.vocal_range: Multiple lead voices; primary range spans baritone to tenor (male) and mezzo-soprano (female)
properties.cultural_impact: Arcade Fire helped bring orchestral, anthemic indie rock to mainstream awareness in the 2000s; their debut Funeral is widely cited as a landmark indie release and The Suburbs won the 2011 Grammy Award for Album of the Year. They've influenced the scale and ambition of contemporary indie bands, raised the profile of Montreal's music scene, and are noted for politically conscious statements and immersive live shows.
properties.performance_style: Large-scale, theatrical and communal live shows featuring multi-instrumental switching, crowd participation, dense arrangements and dramatic climaxes; performances often emphasize emotional immediacy and spectacle.

Their songs often combine personal narrative with communal or generational perspective, balancing intimacy and widescreen commentary.

properties.vocals: Billy Corgan's vocals are high-placed and often nasal, capable of fragile, plaintive tones and forceful, raspy wails; recordings frequently use multi-tracked harmonies and overdubs to create rich, layered vocal textures. Backing vocals and contrast come from other members (notably James Iha) and studio layering contributes to a choir-like, orchestral quality at times.
properties.biography: Formed in Chicago in 1988 by Billy Corgan, The Smashing Pumpkins coalesced around Corgan's songwriting and distinctive voice. Early members James Iha (guitar), D'arcy Wretzky (bass) and Jimmy Chamberlin (drums) helped craft a sound that married heavy, distorted guitars with lush production and melodic hooks. After self-releasing and building a following, the band signed to a major label and released Gish (1991), which led to the breakthrough Siamese Dream (1993). Their 1995 double album Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness cemented their commercial and critical stature. Personnel shifts, interpersonal tensions and changing musical directions led to a breakup in 2000; Billy Corgan later revived the project (2006 onward) with new and returning members, continuing to record and tour while exploring more electronic and orchestral approaches alongside the classic Pumpkins guitar roar.
properties.known_for: Dense, layered guitar arrangements, sweeping dynamics from quiet to loud, ambitious concept albums, memorable melodies, and Billy Corgan's distinctive songwriting and vocals.
properties.description: The Smashing Pumpkins are an American alternative rock band formed in Chicago in 1988, led by singer-songwriter and guitarist Billy Corgan. They rose to international fame in the early 1990s with dense, guitar-layered albums such as Gish (1991), Siamese Dream (1993) and the double LP Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness (1995). Known for blending heavy distortion, orchestral elements and melody, the band produced enduring singles like "Today," "1979," "Bullet With Butterfly Wings" and "Tonight, Tonight." The Pumpkins have undergone multiple lineup changes and hiatuses, experimented with electronic and orchestral textures on later records, and reunited in various forms while maintaining a strong legacy in alternative rock.
properties.cultural_impact: The Smashing Pumpkins defined much of 1990s alternative rock with a sound that fused heavy guitar walls, melodic songwriting and ambitious album-scale concepts; their commercial success helped bring layered, artful rock to mainstream audiences. Iconic videos and large-scale visuals expanded alt-rock's aesthetic, and their production techniques (dense overdubs, layered guitars and orchestral integration) influenced subsequent alternative and indie bands. Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness remains a landmark of the decade, and Billy Corgan's public persona and prolific output have kept the band culturally visible across generations.
properties.performance_style: Live shows blend heavy, guitar-driven climaxes with quieter, orchestral or acoustic passages; performances are often theatrical and visually focused, featuring multi-guitar textures, dramatic dynamics and Billy Corgan's commanding frontman presence.

Themes range from intimate confessions and relationship struggles to broader reflections on fame, disillusionment and nostalgia; imagery can be surreal, melancholic and dramatic, frequently balancing vulnerability with anger.

properties.biography: Formed in New York City in 1998, The Strokes coalesced from a close-knit group of friends and musicians who began playing local clubs and developing a distinctive, guitar-forward sound. Early demos and energetic live shows generated underground buzz, and their 2001 debut, Is This It, became a landmark album: lauded for its immediacy, songwriting and lo-fi sheen. Over the following two decades the band released a string of studio albums, evolving sonically while retaining their core of tight interlocking guitars and Julian Casablancas's idiosyncratic vocal delivery. They helped reshape mainstream rock at the turn of the century, spawning a wave of similarly styled indie acts and remaining active with touring and new releases.
properties.known_for: Pioneering the early-2000s garage rock revival, tight interlocking guitar parts, Julian Casablancas's distinctive vocal delivery, and the landmark debut album Is This It.
properties.description: The Strokes are a New York City rock band formed in 1998 that became central to the early-2000s garage rock revival. Their 2001 debut album Is This It earned widespread critical praise and established the band’s spare, melodic guitar-driven sound, Julian Casablancas’s detached vocal style, and a cool-yet-urban aesthetic. Across several albums — including Room on Fire, First Impressions of Earth, Angles, Comedown Machine and The New Abnormal — they balanced retro influences with concise pop hooks and modern production, influencing a generation of indie and alternative rock bands.
properties.vocal_range: Baritone, Warm Gritty Timbre, Approx E2–A4
properties.cultural_impact: The Strokes helped ignite the early-2000s garage rock and indie rock resurgence, influencing fashion and the sound of alternative rock globally; their debut album is frequently cited as a touchstone that inspired numerous successful bands and reshaped mainstream rock's aesthetic toward leaner, guitar-driven arrangements.
properties.performance_style: Focused, no-frills live shows with tight musicianship and strong guitar interplay; stage presence tends toward cool detachment rather than theatricality, emphasizing song delivery and groove.

properties.biography: Interpol formed in 1997 when guitarist Daniel Kessler met drummer Greg Drudy at New York University; Kessler later recruited Carlos D. (Carlos Dengler) on bass from a history class and reunited with Paul Banks, a friend he'd met in Paris, to complete the early lineup. Drummer Sam Fogarino replaced Drudy in 2000. The band released a string of influential records in the 2000s, most notably Turn On the Bright Lights and Antics, helping define the post-punk revival and the New York indie sound. Dengler, who also contributed keyboards, departed in 2010; since then Banks, Kessler and Fogarino have continued as the creative core, writing and recording while using additional musicians for live performances.
properties.known_for: Dark, brooding post-punk revival sound defined by staccato basslines, interlocking rhythmic guitars, snare-heavy production and Paul Banks's baritone vocals; influential on 2000s indie rock.
properties.description: Interpol is an American rock band formed in Manhattan, New York, in 1997. The core lineup is Paul Banks (vocals, guitar), Daniel Kessler (guitar, backing vocals) and Sam Fogarino (drums). They were a central act in the post-punk revival of the early 2000s, blending staccato basslines, interlocking rhythmic guitars, snare-forward production and baritone-led vocals to create a moody, atmospheric sound. Key albums include Turn On the Bright Lights (2002), Antics (2004), Our Love to Admire (2007), Interpol (2010), El Pintor (2014), Marauder (2018) and The Other Side of Make-Believe (2022). Original bassist Carlos Dengler left in 2010 and has not been permanently replaced; touring and session players have handled bass and keys since.
properties.cultural_impact: Interpol helped define the post-punk revival of the early 2000s and were pivotal to the New York indie scene, influencing a generation of bands that adopted a darker, more atmospheric take on guitar rock. Their aesthetic and sound broadened mainstream acceptance of moody, artful indie rock and their records remain touchstones for post-punk-influenced acts worldwide.
properties.performance_style: Tight, controlled and stoic stage presence with minimal banter; performances emphasize precise interplay, atmosphere and song dynamics rather than showmanship.

properties.lyrical_themes_description: Interpol's lyrics are often oblique and evocative rather than literal, exploring urban alienation, melancholic relationships, memory and introspection. Lines tend to favor atmosphere and suggestion, creating ambiguous narratives that echo the band's brooding musical textures.

properties.vocals: Ben Gibbard's vocals are a clear, earnest tenor with a slightly breathy, intimate timbre; delivery is conversational and affective, often doubled or harmonized in layers to create warm, melancholic textures.
properties.biography: Formed in Bellingham, Washington, in 1997, Death Cab for Cutie began as Ben Gibbard's lo-fi project and soon solidified into a full band with Chris Walla and Nick Harmer among early members. The group moved into the Seattle scene and released a series of critically praised indie records on Barsuk Records. Their fourth album, Transatlanticism (2003), garnered wide attention for its sweeping arrangements and emotional scope; the follow-up, Plans (2005), expanded their audience with radio and chart success. Over time the lineup evolved—most notably Chris Walla's departure in 2014—and the band continued releasing records and touring, balancing intimate acoustic songs with fuller, studio-crafted productions.
properties.known_for: Introspective, literate songwriting paired with melodic arrangements and Ben Gibbard's intimate tenor; known for blending indie sensibilities with polished alternative production and poignant acoustic ballads.
properties.description: Death Cab for Cutie is an American indie rock band formed in Bellingham, Washington in 1997. Fronted by singer-songwriter Ben Gibbard, the band blends literate, emotionally direct lyrics with melodic guitar- and piano-based arrangements. They rose from the Pacific Northwest indie scene to international prominence in the 2000s with albums such as Transatlanticism (2003) and Plans (2005), merging intimate singer-songwriter sensibilities with polished alternative-rock production.
notable_songs: I Will Follow You Into The Dark
properties.cultural_impact: Death Cab for Cutie played a key role in bringing literate, emotionally direct indie rock to a wider audience in the 2000s, bridging college-radio credibility and mainstream visibility; their work influenced a generation of singer-songwriter and indie acts and helped normalize intimate, confessional songwriting in alternative rock and soundtrack placements across film and television.
properties.performance_style: Measured, emotionally-focused live shows that mix quiet, intimate acoustic moments with more energetic, full-band rock numbers; performances emphasize dynamics and lyrical delivery over theatrics.

properties.lyrical_themes_description: Death Cab's lyrics frequently explore personal relationships, loneliness, mortality and the nuances of emotional life; songs balance concrete domestic imagery with abstract reflection, often focused on memory, regret, longing and the small crises of everyday existence.

properties.vocals: Lead vocals primarily by Black Francis with a distinctive, yowling, urgent delivery; former bassist Kim Deal provided contrasting melodic backing and occasional lead vocals. Vocals emphasize tension and contrast—fragile melody against abrasive textures—and make frequent use of harmony, call-and-response and shouted phrases.
properties.biography: Formed in Boston in 1986 by Black Francis (vocals, guitar) and Joey Santiago (lead guitar) and soon joined by Kim Deal (bass, vocals) and David Lovering (drums), Pixies quickly established a distinctive sound combining punk ferocity, surf-rock guitar lines and pop melody. Their early releases—Come On Pilgrim (1987) and Surfer Rosa (1988, produced by Steve Albini)—garnered critical attention; the follow-up Doolittle (1989) cemented their reputation with widespread critical praise. Despite limited mainstream commercial success in the U.S., they cultivated a strong following in Europe and among alternative radio and critics. Tensions led to a 1993 split; members pursued other projects (Frank Black solo, The Breeders). The band reunited in 2004 for touring and subsequent recording, releasing new material and continuing to influence generations of alternative musicians.
properties.known_for: Pioneering quiet-loud dynamics, surreal and cryptic lyrics, influential late-1980s/early-1990s albums (Surfer Rosa, Doolittle) and a major role in shaping alternative rock and grunge.
properties.description: Pixies are an American alternative rock band formed in Boston in 1986. Known for their loud-quiet-loud dynamics, surreal and often cryptic lyrics, and a blend of melodic hooks with abrasive guitar textures, they released seminal records including Come On Pilgrim (EP), Surfer Rosa, Doolittle, Bossanova and Trompe le Monde. They split in 1993, reunited in 2004 and have continued to record and tour with lineup changes (notably Kim Deal on bass and vocals until 2013, Paz Lenchantin 2016–2024, and Emma Richardson joining in 2024). Frequently cited as a key influence on the alternative and grunge explosion of the early 1990s, their combination of punk energy, surf-rock riffs and pop sensibility left a lasting mark on alternative music worldwide.
properties.cultural_impact: Pixies are widely credited with shaping the sound and sensibility of alternative rock in the late 1980s and early 1990s; their quiet-loud-quiet dynamics and mix of melody with abrasiveness influenced grunge and countless alternative bands (most famously Nirvana). Albums like Doolittle are regarded as touchstones of indie rock; their influence persists in modern alternative, indie and rock acts and in the canon of critically acclaimed independent music.
properties.performance_style: Live shows emphasize stark dynamics (quiet verses, explosive choruses), raw energy and a direct stage presence; performances can be terse and intense with occasional offbeat humor.

Black Francis often wrote vivid, fragmentary narratives that leave interpretation open.

properties.vocals: Rivers Cuomo is the primary lead vocalist with a youthful, slightly nasal tenor tone characterized by clear enunciation and emotive, often confessional delivery. Backing and occasional lead vocals come from Brian Bell and Scott Shriner, providing tight harmonies and call-and-response textures. Vocals range from bright, hook-forward pop phrasing to quieter, melancholic moments and more aggressive, shout-y rock passages.
properties.biography: Weezer formed in Los Angeles in 1992 when Rivers Cuomo joined forces with Patrick Wilson, Matt Sharp and Jason Cropper; web/archivist Karl Koch became an early associate. After playing small L.A. clubs and circulating demos, the band signed to DGC/Geffen in June 1993. Their 1994 self-titled debut (The Blue Album), produced by Ric Ocasek, delivered hits like "Undone (The Sweater Song)", "Buddy Holly" and "Say It Ain't So" and established their blend of power-pop hooks and alternative rock. Following early lineup changes (Brian Bell replacing Jason Cropper, later Mikey Welsh and then Scott Shriner on bass), Weezer weathered critical ups and downs — the initially maligned Pinkerton became a cult classic — and continued to experiment across pop, hard-rock and orchestral arrangements while maintaining a distinct nerdy/earnest persona.
properties.known_for: Catchy, hook-heavy songwriting with an earnest, geeky persona; influential 1990s albums (The Blue Album, Pinkerton), memorable MTV-era videos ("Buddy Holly"), stylistic variety and long-term commercial success.
properties.description: Weezer is an American alternative rock band formed in Los Angeles in 1992. Fronted by Rivers Cuomo with Patrick Wilson, and early members Matt Sharp and Jason Cropper (later Brian Bell), the band broke through with their self-titled 1994 debut ("The Blue Album") and the MTV-era singles and videos that followed. Their career spans diverse styles — power-pop hooks, heavier guitar rock (Van Weezer), orchestral chamber-pop (OK Human), and seasonal EPs (the 2022 SZNZ series) — and includes commercially successful albums, a cult-classic (Pinkerton), and more than 35 million records sold worldwide.
properties.cultural_impact: Weezer helped popularize a melodic, nerd-friendly strain of 1990s alternative rock and power pop; their MTV-era videos (notably "Buddy Holly") and accessible hooks brought them mainstream attention. Pinkerton's critical reappraisal influenced generations of emo/indie songwriters, and the band's willingness to experiment—shifting between hard-rock riffs, orchestral arrangements and pop collaborations—has kept them culturally relevant across multiple decades.
properties.performance_style: Live shows are tight, guitar-forward and hook-focused, mixing high-energy renditions of hits with deeper cuts; performances often include playful banter, occasional theatrical or humorous elements, acoustic or orchestral arrangements on special shows, and active fan engagement.

short_descriptions.value: Weezer es una banda de rock estadounidense conocida por sus melodías pegadizas y su estética geek rock.

properties.lyrical_themes_description: Weezer's lyrics—principally written by Rivers Cuomo—often blend confessional, autobiographical details with themes of awkwardness, unrequited love, teenage longing and nostalgia. They can range from earnest and vulnerable (Pinkerton-era material) to tongue-in-cheek or satirical (some later singles), and sometimes deploy conceptual or narrative framing (e.g., the abandoned Songs From The Black Hole concept).

properties.vocals: Vocals are primarily provided by Damon Albarn (as the voice behind 2-D) with recurring lead contributions from fictional character Noodle and guest vocalists. Performances vary between Albarn's relaxed, melodic delivery, guest rappers' rhythmic verses, soulful duet parts and layered background harmonies; the project's vocal approach is collaborative and stylistically diverse rather than centered on a single defined range.
properties.biography: Gorillaz began in 1998 when Blur frontman Damon Albarn and cartoonist Jamie Hewlett — then roommates in London — conceived a 'virtual band' as a critique and reimagining of pop music's image culture. Combining Albarn's songwriting with Hewlett's character design, the project presented four animated members with a fully developed fictional history. Their self-titled 2001 debut mixed hip-hop, electronica and pop and sold millions worldwide; Demon Days (2005) consolidated their success with global sales, multiple hit singles and awards. Across subsequent albums (Plastic Beach, The Fall, Humanz, The Now Now, Song Machine and Cracker Island) Gorillaz expanded its collaborative model, working with diverse musicians and using animation, projections and web-driven episodes to tell an ongoing saga that blurs fiction and musical authorship.
properties.known_for: Being a pioneering virtual band that fuses multiple genres, uses animated characters and multimedia storytelling, and collaborates widely with guest artists.
properties.description: Gorillaz is a British virtual band created in 1998 by musician Damon Albarn and artist Jamie Hewlett. Presented as four animated characters — Murdoc Niccals, 2-D, Noodle and Russel Hobbs — the project blends rock, hip-hop, electronic and world music and is defined by high-profile guest collaborations, cinematic visuals and an extensive fictional backstory. Musically flexible and multimedia-focused, Gorillaz has released multiple multi-platinum albums (including Gorillaz and Demon Days), won major awards and popularized a concept-driven, animation-forward approach to a band identity and live presentation.
properties.cultural_impact: Gorillaz redefined what a band identity could be by popularizing a fully realized virtual group that combined animation, narrative worldbuilding and mainstream pop collaborations. They influenced how musicians use multimedia storytelling, remote guest features and immersive visuals; their commercial success helped legitimize experimental cross-genre projects and multimedia marketing in the 21st century. The project won major awards, achieved multi-platinum sales and introduced large-scale projection and avatar-based performance techniques into live music presentation.
properties.performance_style: Live presentations mix real musicians and guest performers with large-scale animation, projections or holographic/3D elements; concerts emphasize spectacle, narrative vignettes and multimedia integration rather than a traditional band fronted solely by visible members.

British virtual band blending rock, hip-hop, electronic and world influences, created by Damon Albarn and Jamie Hewlett and known for animated members and high-profile collaborations.

properties.lyrical_themes_description: Gorillaz lyrics often explore themes of modern alienation, the emptiness of consumer culture and fame, technological mediation of experience, environmental collapse (notably on Plastic Beach), interpersonal relationships and narrative vignettes tied to the band's fictional backstory. The tone ranges from satirical and political to melancholic and introspective.
